present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-canonical-model
present_destinations.title: Canonical-model method
present_destinations.declaration_text:
\index{canonical-model method!modal logic}
For a fixed normal modal logic \(\mathfrak L\), let the worlds be the maximal
\(\mathfrak L\)-consistent sets.  Define the metalinguistic proof relation
\(R_{\mathfrak L}\) by
\[
 \Gamma R_{\mathfrak L}\Delta
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 \forall A\,(\Box A\in\Gamma\to A\in\Delta),
\]
and make an atom true at \(\Gamma\) exactly when it belongs to \(\Gamma\).
This construction is needed to distinguish the proof model from an arbitrary
semantic structure.  Its worlds are theories, unlike filtration worlds, which
are equivalence classes of worlds from a given model.  The relation is used by
the modal existence lemma, truth lemma, and the frame-property checks in the
following adequacy sketch.  The ordinary construction applies to the canonical
systems \(K\), \(KD\), \(KT\), \(KTB\), \(K4\), \(S4\) (\(KT4\)),
\(KD45\), \(S4.2\), \(S4.3\), and \(S5\) with their source-defined
schemas; it is not the completeness route asserted for GL or Grz.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-modal-canonical-completeness
present_destinations.title: Canonical strong completeness for \(K\), \(KT\), \(S4\), and \(S5\)
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For each of the four exact Hilbert sheets
\texttt{sheet:hilbert-k}, \texttt{sheet:hilbert-t},
\texttt{sheet:hilbert-s4}, and \texttt{sheet:hilbert-s5}, derivability from an
arbitrary premise set is equivalent to local consequence over, respectively,
all frames, reflexive frames, reflexive transitive frames, and equivalence
frames.  Necessitation remains theorem-only in premise derivations.

present_destinations.label: annex:p8.modal.1
present_destinations.title: Canonical strong completeness for K, KT, S4, and S5
present_destinations.declaration_text:
\begin{proof}
Fix one of the four Hilbert systems \(L\).  Because necessitation in a
derivation from premises may be applied only to a separately proved theorem,
the ordinary deduction theorem holds: induction on a finite premise derivation
shows that \(\Gamma,A\derives_L B\) implies
\(\Gamma\derives_L A\to B\).  Hence, if
\(\Gamma\not\derives_L A\), the set
\(\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\) is \(L\)-consistent.  Enumerate the formulas and,
at each stage, add the next formula when consistency is preserved and otherwise
add its negation.  The union is a maximal \(L\)-consistent set extending
\(\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\).  This is the Lindenbaum extension used below.

Let \(W_L\) be all maximal \(L\)-consistent sets and define
\[
 wR_Lv
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{B:\Box B\in w\}\subseteq v,
 \qquad
 V(p)=\{w:p\in w\}.
\]
The modal existence lemma says that if \(\neg\Box B\in w\), there is
\(v\in W_L\) with \(wR_Lv\) and \(\neg B\in v\).  Otherwise the set
\(\{C:\Box C\in w\}\cup\{\neg B\}\) would be inconsistent.  Some finite
conjunction \(C_1\land\cdots\land C_n\) of its boxed antecedents would then
prove \(B\).  Theorem-only necessitation, distribution, and propositional
reasoning would put \(\Box B\) in \(w\), contradicting maximal consistency.
Lindenbaum extension of that consistent set gives the required \(v\).

Induction on formulas proves the truth lemma
\[
 M_L,w\models B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\in w.
\]
Boolean cases are the standard maximal-consistency cases.  If \(\Box B\in w\),
the definition of \(R_L\) and the induction hypothesis make \(B\) true at
every successor.  If \(\Box B\notin w\), maximality gives
\(\neg\Box B\in w\), and the existence lemma supplies a successor falsifying
\(B\).  This completes the box case.

The canonical frame has the required property in each extension.  In \(KT\),
\(\Box B\to B\) makes \(wR_Lw\).  In \(S4\), if
\(wR_LvR_Lu\) and \(\Box B\in w\), axiom 4 puts
\(\Box\Box B\in w\), hence \(\Box B\in v\) and \(B\in u\); thus the
relation is transitive.  In \(S5\), reflexivity comes from T.  To prove
Euclideanness, suppose \(wR_Lv,wR_Lu\) and \(\Box B\in v\).  If
\(\Box B\notin w\), then \(\Diamond\neg B\in w\); axiom 5 puts
\(\Box\Diamond\neg B\in w\), so \(\Diamond\neg B\in v\), contradicting
\(\Box B\in v\).  Therefore \(\Box B\in w\), and \(wR_Lu\) gives
\(B\in u\).  Hence \(vR_Lu\).  A reflexive Euclidean relation is symmetric
and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.

Soundness is induction on derivations: the propositional axioms and modus
ponens preserve local validity, K is valid on every frame, theorem-only
necessitation preserves validity, and T, 4, and 5 have the frame properties
just named.  For completeness, if
\(\Gamma\not\derives_L A\), choose the maximal set \(w\) extending
\(\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\).  The truth lemma makes every member of \(\Gamma\)
true at \(w\) and \(A\) false there, on a frame in the required class.  This
contrapositive proves strong completeness for local consequence in all four
rows.
\end{proof}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-filtration
present_destinations.title: Filtration through a finite formula set
present_destinations.declaration_text:
\index{filtration!modal logic}
Fix a finite subformula-closed set \(\Phi\) and a Kripke structure
\(\mathcal M=(W,R,V)\).  Put
\[
 w\sim_{\Phi}u
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 \forall A\in\Phi\,
   (\mathcal M,w\entails A\text{ iff }\mathcal M,u\entails A).
\]
The quotient has worlds \([w]_{\Phi}\), at most \(2^{\lvert\Phi\rvert}\)
of them, and the induced atomic valuation.  The minimal quotient relation
relates \([w]_{\Phi}\) to \([u]_{\Phi}\) when some representatives are
\(R\)-related.  The maximal quotient relation relates them when, for every
\(\Box A\in\Phi\), truth of \(\Box A\) at \(w\) implies truth of \(A\) at
\(u\).  A \emph{filtration relation} is a quotient relation between those two
bounds.  This construction is an image of a given semantic model, unlike the
maximal-consistent-theory construction in
Method~\ref{def:p08-modal-canonical-model}; it is used to preserve truth on
\(\Phi\) while making the model finite.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-modal-filtration
present_destinations.title: Filtration and decidability
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Every filtration as in Method~\ref{def:p08-modal-filtration} preserves the
truth of each formula in \(\Phi\).  For \(K\) use an ordinary filtration
relation; for \(KT\) use its reflexive closure; for \(S4\) use the standard
reflexive-transitive filtration construction; and for \(S5\) use the
equivalence-class construction.
In each case the declared filtration relation remains between the minimal and maximal
bounds and preserves the target frame class.  Hence \(K\), \(KT\), \(S4\),
and \(S5\) have the
finite-model property and are decidable
\cite{BlackburnDeRijkeVenema2001,ChagrovZakharyaschev1997}.  This is cited new
content: no local proof or inherited compression denominator is claimed.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-standard-translation
present_destinations.title: First-order standard translation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For each propositional variable \(p\), choose a unary predicate symbol
\(P_p\).  The standard translation at the displayed free world variable
\(x\), written \(\operatorname{ST}_x\), is the metalinguistic recursion
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{ST}_x(p)&=P_p(x),
 &\operatorname{ST}_x(\bottom)&=\bottom,\\
 \operatorname{ST}_x(\neg A)&=\neg\operatorname{ST}_x(A),
 &\operatorname{ST}_x(A\circ B)&=
   \operatorname{ST}_x(A)\circ\operatorname{ST}_x(B),\\
 \operatorname{ST}_x(\Box A)&=
   \forall y\,(Rxy\to\operatorname{ST}_y(A)),
 &\operatorname{ST}_x(\Diamond A)&=
   \exists y\,(Rxy\land\operatorname{ST}_y(A)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to\}\) and \(y\) is fresh.  This is a
translation into first-order formulas over the frame relation and valuation
predicates, not a new modal connective.  It is needed to state the exact frame
conditions below and later to formulate the bisimulation characterization.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-modal-correspondence
present_destinations.title: Elementary modal frame correspondences
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every Kripke frame, validity of each named schema in the first column of
Table~\ref{tab:p08-modal-correspondence} is equivalent to the displayed
first-order condition on its accessibility relation.  The row named B concerns
the B schema alone; the displayed system \(KTB\) additionally contains T and
hence uses reflexive symmetric frames.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-sahlqvist-class
present_destinations.title: The Sahlqvist class used here
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Rewrite modal formulas using \(\bottom,\topv,\neg,\land,\lor,\Box,\Diamond\).
An occurrence of a variable is positive when it lies under an even number of
negations and negative when it lies under an odd number.  A \emph{boxed atom}
is \(\Box^n p\) for \(n\geq0\).  A \emph{Sahlqvist antecedent} is generated
from boxed atoms, formulas all of whose variable occurrences are negative,
and \(\bottom,\topv\) by \(\land,\lor,\Diamond\).  A \emph{Sahlqvist
implication} has such an antecedent and a consequent all of whose variable
occurrences are positive; finite conjunctions of these implications form the
Sahlqvist class fixed here.  This exact syntactic class is narrower than the
class of all modal formulas and is introduced because the following theorem
does not hold for arbitrary schemas.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-sahlqvist
present_destinations.title: Sahlqvist theorem
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Every formula in the class fixed by
Definition~\ref{def:p08-sahlqvist-class} has an effectively computable
first-order frame correspondent, is canonical, and axiomatizes a normal modal
logic complete for the corresponding elementary frame class.  No claim is
made here that an arbitrary modal axiom is a Sahlqvist formula.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-bisimulation
present_destinations.title: Bisimulation of pointed Kripke structures

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-modal-bisimulation-invariance
present_destinations.title: Bisimulation invariance
present_destinations.declaration_text:
If \(wZw'\) for a bisimulation between \(\mathcal M\) and \(\mathcal N\),
then for every basic modal formula \(A\),
\[
 \mathcal M,w\entails A
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 \mathcal N,w'\entails A.
\]

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-van-benthem
present_destinations.title: Van Benthem characterization theorem
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Over all Kripke structures, a first-order formula with one free world variable
is equivalent to \(\operatorname{ST}_x(A)\) for some basic modal formula
\(A\) exactly when it is invariant under bisimulations.  This statement is not
restricted to finite structures; the finite-model version is a different
theorem.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-b-convention
present_destinations.title: The system \(KTB\), the schema B, and the alias \(B\)
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Chellas writes \(KTB\) for the reflexive symmetric modal-cube system: it
contains both the T schema and the B schema.  The B schema alone corresponds
to symmetry, and Chellas writes \(KB\) for the strictly weaker system obtained
by adding only that schema to \(K\) \cite{Chellas1980}.  Hughes and Cresswell
use \(B\) as a name for the reflexive symmetric system
\cite{HughesCresswell1996}; here \(B\) is therefore recorded only as their
source-bound alias for the card whose Chellas name is \(KTB\).

present_destinations.label: def:p08-tense-until-since
present_destinations.title: Kamp's strict U and S operators
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \((T,<,V)\) be a linearly ordered temporal structure.  The strict binary
future and past constructors have the clauses
\[
\begin{aligned}
 t\entails U\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u>t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(t<v<u\to v\entails B)],\\
 t\entails S\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u<t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(u<v<t\to v\entails B)].
\end{aligned}
\]
The prefix symbols \(U\) and \(S\) are Kamp's binary future and past formula
constructors, respectively.  Their first operand holds at the witness and
their second operand at every intervening point; they are not metalinguistic
English tense.  They
are needed because Prior's unary future/past operators cannot express all
one-variable first-order order properties.  Their strict witnesses and two
directions distinguish them from the non-strict discrete LTL until fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:modal-temporal-epistemic-02}; the following theorem uses them
\cite{Prior1967,Kamp1968}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-kamp
present_destinations.title: Kamp expressive completeness with its order hypothesis
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Kamp's compositional map sends every formula using negation, conjunction, and
his strict \(U,S\) to an equivalent one-free-variable formula in the displayed
first-order language with \(<\) and unary predicates; its truth induction is
valid over every binary structure.  Conversely, over Kamp's class
\(\mathsf{Com}\) of strict linear orders, every uniformly
first-order-definable tense is expressible by such a temporal formula.
\(\mathsf{Com}\) requires greatest lower and least upper bounds for every
nonempty bounded set; it permits discrete orders and endpoints and does not
mean deductive completeness.  The reverse translation is primitive recursive,
but the thesis gives no complexity or output-size bound.  It is not asserted
over all linear orders; Kamp's rational-order Theorem~IV.5 supplies a
counterexample to this four-operation basis.  The full source presentation is
Section~\ref{sec:p09-presentation-n-c-012}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-modal-fusion
present_destinations.title: Fusion of normal modal logics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For normal modal logics \(L_1,L_2\) in disjoint modal signatures, their
\emph{fusion} is the least normal multimodal logic containing the theorem sets
of both components and no interaction axioms.  Its standing is a construction
on logics, not a connective.  The name is necessary to distinguish mere
 side-by-side combination from products, commutation principles, and tense
 systems whose past and future relations are converses; that nonredundancy is
 used in the following comparison.  In particular, placing independent future
 and past logics side by side gives their fusion, whereas requiring their frame
 relations to be converses adds an interaction condition and no longer gives a
 pure fusion.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-ockhamist-peircean
present_destinations.title: Ockhamist and Peircean branching-time evaluation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
On a branching order, a \emph{history} is a maximal linearly ordered set of
moments.  Ockhamist future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment--history pair,
so it can depend on the current history through that moment.  Peircean
future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment and quantifies over branching
futures.  These are semantic evaluation policies, not competing names for CTL
path quantifiers.  Their different evaluation points prevent ambiguity, and
the distinction is used to delimit the computational cards above from this
philosophical survey \cite{Burgess1984}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-neighborhood-model
present_destinations.title: Neighborhood model
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{neighborhood model} is
\(\mathcal M=(W,N,V)\), where \(W\ne\varnothing\),
\(V:\mathsf{Prop}\to\mathcal P(W)\), and
\(N:W\to\mathcal P(\mathcal P(W))\).  For a formula \(A\), define
its truth-set abbreviation by
\(\lbrack\!\lbrack A\rbrack\!\rbrack_{\mathcal M}
\defeq\{w\in W:\mathcal M,w\entails A\}\).  The modal clause is
\[
 \mathcal M,w\entails\Box A
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 \lbrack\!\lbrack A\rbrack\!\rbrack_{\mathcal M}\in N(w).
\]
The function \(N\) is needed because a single accessibility relation
cannot represent every congruential non-normal logic.  Its standing is a
semantic assignment of proposition sets to each world; it is neither the
system \(EN\) nor the set of normal worlds used in the later
Routley--Meyer structure.  It differs from a Kripke
relation by taking subsets of \(W\), rather than worlds, as its local semantic
arguments, and is used in all five cards below
\cite{Scott1970,Montague1970,Chellas1980,Pacuit2017}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-neighborhood-conditions
present_destinations.title: Neighborhood closure conditions
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every world \(w\) and \(X,Y\subseteq W\), call \(N\)
\emph{upward closed} when
\(X\in N(w)\) and \(X\subseteq Y\) imply
\(Y\in N(w)\); \emph{binary-intersection closed} when
\(X,Y\in N(w)\) implies
\(X\cap Y\in N(w)\); and \emph{unit containing} when
\(W\in N(w)\).  These are semantic frame conditions, not additional
object-language rules.  They are introduced separately because Chellas's
schemas M, C, and N determine different combinations of them
\cite{Chellas1980,Pacuit2017}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-qml-family
present_destinations.title: Quantified modal logic is a parameterized family
present_destinations.declaration_text:
There is no single calculus or semantics determined by the phrase
``quantified modal logic.''  A source presentation must specify its
propositional modal base, quantifier rules, domain variation, designation
policy, and local or global consequence.  The clauses below reproduce
Fitting's model and quantifier notation for the limited purpose of comparing
the actualist Barcan schemas; Garson is used only for the surrounding
comparison with other quantified-modal presentations.  No hybrid calculus or
system card is inferred from that semantic example
\cite{Fitting2002Alethic,FittingMendelsohn1998,Garson2001}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-qml-model
present_destinations.title: Fitting's varying-domain modal model
present_destinations.declaration_text:
In Fitting's notation a model is
\[
 \mathcal M=\langle\mathcal G,\mathcal R,\mathcal D,\mathcal I\rangle,
\]
where \(\mathcal G\) is a nonempty set of worlds,
\(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal G^2\), and
\(\mathcal D\) maps each \(\Gamma\in\mathcal G\) to a nonempty world-domain
\(\mathcal D(\Gamma)\).  The domain of the model is
\(\bigcup_{\Gamma\in\mathcal G}\mathcal D(\Gamma)\).  The interpretation
\(\mathcal I\) maps each predicate symbol \(P\) to its world-relative
extension \(\mathcal I(P)(\Gamma)\) over that model domain and each individual
constant \(c\) to a world-indexed denotation
\(\mathcal I(c)(\Gamma)\) in the model domain.  A constant is a
\emph{rigid designator} exactly when some \(d\) satisfies
\(\mathcal I(c)(\Gamma)=d\) at every world \(\Gamma\).  Rigidity concerns
cross-world identity of denotation; whether \(d\in\mathcal D(\Gamma)\) is the
separate actual-existence question expressed by \(E(c)\).  The Barcan formulas
below contain variables rather than constants, so their proof uses the fixed
valuation convention and does not assume that every name is rigid.
The term is necessary because a world-independent variable assignment does not
fix the denotation policy for names.  Its standing is a property of a constant's
interpretation, and its nonredundancy from existence is used when rigid names
denote objects outside a current world-domain.  For Fitting's special
existence predicate \(E\),
\[
 \mathcal I(E)(\Gamma)=\mathcal D(\Gamma).
\]
Valuations \(v\) take variables into the model domain and do not vary with the
world.  For a formula \(\Phi\), truth is written
\(\mathcal M,\Gamma\forces_v\Phi\).  Ordinary
\((\forall x)\) and \((\exists x)\) are possibilist and range over the whole
model domain.  Fitting's actualist quantifiers are the exact abbreviations
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (\forall^{E}x)\Phi
 &\defeq (\forall x)[E(x)\supset\Phi],\\
 (\exists^{E}x)\Phi
 &\defeq (\exists x)[E(x)\land\Phi].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the relativized quantifiers range over \(\mathcal D(\Gamma)\) at world
\(\Gamma\), while modal satisfaction keeps \(v\) fixed when it moves along
\(\mathcal R\).  The model-domain convention is necessary to state
decreasing-domain failures with one world-independent valuation
\cite{Fitting2002Alethic,FittingMendelsohn1998}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-qml-domain-regimes
present_destinations.title: Domain regimes and philosophical readings
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The domains are \emph{constant} when \(\mathcal D(\Gamma)\) has the same
value at every world; \emph{increasing} when
\(\Gamma\mathcal R\Delta\) implies
\(\mathcal D(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathcal D(\Delta)\);
\emph{decreasing} when \(\Gamma\mathcal R\Delta\) implies
\(\mathcal D(\Delta)\subseteq\mathcal D(\Gamma)\); and
\emph{arbitrarily varying} when no inclusion condition is imposed.  In this
section, \emph{actualist quantification} means Fitting's relativized
\(\forall^E,\exists^E\), while the primitive unrelativized quantifiers are
\emph{possibilist}; and the domain assignment is \emph{necessitist} exactly
when every world-domain is the whole model domain.  These are explicitly defined
interpretations of the semantic parameters, not consequences of the validity
table below.  The displayed BF/CBF table uses the actualist clauses.  Under
possibilist quantification over the model domain, varying the world-domains does not
generate that table; under necessitism, actualist and possibilist
quantification coincide with the constant-domain case.  This is the later use
that requires the three readings to remain distinct \cite{Williamson2013}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-barcan-schemas
present_destinations.title: Barcan and converse Barcan schemas
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For a formula \(\Phi(x)\), the actualist \emph{Barcan formula}
\((\mathrm{BF}^{E})\) and actualist \emph{converse Barcan formula}
\((\mathrm{CBF}^{E})\) in Fitting's notation are respectively
\[
 (\forall^{E}x)\Box\Phi(x)\to\Box(\forall^{E}x)\Phi(x),
 \qquad
 \Box(\forall^{E}x)\Phi(x)\to(\forall^{E}x)\Box\Phi(x).
\]
The superscript records that this table uses the source's actualist
relativization.  With the primitive possibilist quantifier, local-domain
variation does not yield the table below.  The two names remain in this order;
their difference
is used in Table~\ref{tab:p08-barcan-domains} and
Figure~\ref{fig:p08-barcan-countermodel}; they are not interchanged when the
domain convention changes \cite{Barcan1946}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-barcan-domain-validities
present_destinations.title: Actualist Barcan validity in Fitting's model
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Under Definitions~\ref{def:p08-qml-model}--\ref{def:p08-barcan-schemas}, the
validity pattern is exactly that displayed in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-barcan-domains}.  The decreasing-domain row uses the fixed
outer domain and fixed-variable-assignment convention; without such a convention the
reversal is not a well-formed comparison.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-distributed-knowledge
present_destinations.title: Distributed knowledge for a finite group
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(G\subseteq I\) be nonempty and finite.  In the multi-agent epistemic
model with agent relations \(\sim_i\), define
\[
 R_G^{D}\defeq\bigcap_{i\in G}\sim_i,
 \qquad
 \mathcal M,w\models D_GA
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall u\,(wR_G^{D}u\Rightarrow\mathcal M,u\models A).
\]
The name is necessary because pooled information can determine \(A\) even
when no individual agent knows it.  It names a group modality, not a new frame
relation for an individual agent.  It differs from
\(E_GA\defeq\bigwedge_{i\in G}K_iA\), which uses the union of one-step agent
alternatives, and from \(C_GA\), which uses the reflexive--transitive closure
of that union.  The distinction is used by the card and comparison table below
\cite{FaginHalpernMosesVardi1995}.
\index{distributed knowledge}\index{group knowledge}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-public-announcement
present_destinations.title: Truthful public-announcement update
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For an epistemic structure \(\mathcal M\), let
\(\mathcal M\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\chi\) be the substructure induced by the worlds where
\(\chi\) is true.  The public-announcement modality has the clause
\[
 \mathcal M,w\entails[!\chi]A
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 \bigl(\mathcal M,w\not\entails\chi\ \lor\
       \mathcal M\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\chi,w\entails A\bigr),
\]
and \(\langle!\chi\rangle A\defeq\neg[!\chi]\neg A\).  The update is a
model restriction, not a change to the valuation at surviving worlds.  Its
standing and vacuous-failure clause distinguish announcement from ordinary
knowledge and are used by the reduction theorem and the unsuccessful-update
example.  General event-model product update is broader and is not identified
with this operation \cite{Plaza1989,BaltagMossSolecki1998}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-pal-reduction
present_destinations.title: Reduction of public announcements
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Over the exact finite-agent \(\mathsf{S5}_{I}\) base fixed by
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-s5n]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-s5n}}, every public-announcement
formula is provably equivalent, using
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-pal]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-pal}}, to an
announcement-free epistemic formula.  Hence the reduction calculus is sound
and complete for the update semantics of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-public-announcement}.  This does not reduce arbitrary
action-model logic to the same static language
\cite{VanDitmarschVanDerHoekKooi2007}.

present_destinations.label: entry:p08-pal
present_destinations.title: Public announcement logic PAL

present_destinations.label: def:p08-unsuccessful-announcement
present_destinations.title: An unsuccessful truthful update
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Call \(\chi\) \emph{successful} when \([!\chi]\chi\) is valid.  This is a
metalinguistic property of an announcement formula, needed to distinguish
preservation of announced content from mere executability; it is not another
modality, differs from truth before an update, and is used in this example.
Let two worlds \(w,v\) be indistinguishable to agent \(i\), with \(p\) true
only at \(w\).  At \(w\), \(\chi=p\land\neg K_ip\) is true.  Restricting to
the \(\chi\)-world leaves only \(w\), where \(K_ip\) is now true, so \(\chi\)
is false after its own truthful announcement.  Thus truth before update does
not entail success \cite{VanDitmarschVanDerHoekKooi2007}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-heyting-algebra
present_destinations.title: Heyting algebra and formula valuation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{Heyting algebra} is a bounded distributive lattice

\[
  \mathcal H=(H,\wedge,\vee,0,1,\Rightarrow)
\]

whose final binary operation is characterized, for all \(a,b,c\in H\), by

\[
  a\wedge b\leq c
  \quad\text{exactly when}\quad
  a\leq b\Rightarrow c.
\]

In this definition the source symbols \(\wedge,\vee,0,1,\Rightarrow\) are
typed as Heyting-algebra operations and bounds; in particular,
\(\Rightarrow\) is not the sequent arrow and not the object-language
conditional.  A formula valuation is a map
\(\nu:\mathsf{Prop}\to H\), extended by
\(\nu(\bottom)=0\), by the lattice meet and join for
\(\land,\lor\), and by
\(\nu(A\to B)=\nu(A)\Rightarrow\nu(B)\).
Algebraic negation is
\(\neg a\defeq a\Rightarrow0\).

This structure is needed to distinguish algebraic validity from Kripke
forcing.  Boolean algebras are the special Heyting algebras in which every
\(a\vee\neg a=1\); general Heyting
algebras need not satisfy that equation.  The distinction is used by the
IPL/CPL comparison and the intermediate-logics table below.
\index{Heyting algebra}
\index{semantics!algebraic!intuitionistic}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-heyting-completeness
present_destinations.title: Heyting-algebra completeness for IPL
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every propositional formula \(A\),
\(\derives_{\mathsf{IPL}}A\) exactly when every valuation in every Heyting
algebra assigns \(A\) the top value \(1\).

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-heyting-completeness
present_destinations.title: Algebraic completeness of IPC
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The algebra \(H_{\mathsf{IPC}}\) is a nontrivial Heyting algebra.
For every formula \(\varphi\),
\[
 \vdash_{\mathsf{IPC}}\varphi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\varphi]=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_v^H=1_H
       \text{ for every Heyting algebra }H\text{ and valuation }v.
\]
The canonical valuation \(v_0(p)=[p]\) gives
\(\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_{v_0}=[\varphi]\), and therefore
refutes every non-theorem.
More generally, for a finite premise set \(\Gamma\),
\[
 \Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{IPC}}\varphi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigwedge_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\llbracket\gamma\rrbracket_v^H
       \leq\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_v^H
       \text{ for every }H,v.
\]
The empty meet is \(1\).

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-heyting-prime-representation
present_destinations.title: Prime-filter representation and the implication witness
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Assume BPIT.  For every Heyting algebra \(H\), the map
\[
 \beta_H:H\longrightarrow
       \operatorname{Up}(\operatorname{Pf}(H),\subseteq)
\]
is an injective Heyting homomorphism.
In particular, for \(a,b\in H\) and \(P\in\operatorname{Pf}(H)\),
\[
 a\Rightarrow b\in P
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall Q\supseteq P\
       (Q\in\operatorname{Pf}(H)\text{ and }a\in Q
                     \Longrightarrow b\in Q).
\]
If \(a\Rightarrow b\notin P\), a witnessing prime filter
\(Q\supseteq P\) contains \(a\) and omits \(b\).
If \(H\) is nontrivial, its prime-filter order is nonempty.
For trivial \(H\), it is empty and the displayed map is the
isomorphism between two one-element algebras.
For countable \(H\), these conclusions hold in ZF using the
countable case of Theorem~\ref{thm:p10-prime-filter-separation}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-ipc-prime-kripke-completeness
present_destinations.title: Strong local Kripke completeness of IPC
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Assume BPIT for an arbitrary variable set.
For every formula set \(\Gamma\) and formula \(\varphi\),
\[
 \Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{IPC}}\varphi
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Gamma\entails_{\mathsf{IPL}}\varphi
\]
with the persistent valuations, nonempty preorders, and local
forcing convention of
Definitions~\ref{def:p08-ipl-kripke-structure}--\ref{def:p08-ipl-consequence}.
The same equivalence holds if frames are required to be partial orders.
Every failure of derivability is witnessed on the prime filters
of \(H_{\mathsf{IPC}}\), ordered by inclusion, with
\[
 V(p)=\beta_{H_{\mathsf{IPC}}}([p]).
\]
If the variable set is countable, the entire argument works in
ZF by the countable prime-filter-separation theorem.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-rasiowa-sikorski
present_destinations.title: Rasiowa--Sikorski lemma
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \((P,\leq)\) be a nonempty poset, let \(p\in P\), and let
\(\mathcal D\) be a countable family of downward dense subsets of
\(P\), where countable includes finite.
Under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}\), there is a
\(\mathcal D\)-generic filter \(G\) containing \(p\).

If \(\mathcal D=\{D_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is given by a sequence,
one can take
\[
\begin{gathered}
 p_0=p,\qquad p_{n+1}\leq p_n,\qquad p_{n+1}\in D_n,\\
 G=\{q\in P:\exists n\in\mathbb N\quad p_n\leq q\}.
\end{gathered}
\]
If \(P\) has a fixed enumeration \(e:\mathbb N\to P\) onto it,
the same conclusion is provable in \(\mathsf{ZF}\) alone, by always
using the first enumerated suitable extension.
For a finite family \(\mathcal D\), \(\mathsf{ZF}\) suffices even
when \(P\) is arbitrary.  If \(P\) is finite, a filter containing
\(p\) can meet every downward dense subset of \(P\) at once in
\(\mathsf{ZF}\).

present_destinations.label: def:p08-ipl-topological-semantics
present_destinations.title: Open-set semantics for IPL
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(X\) be a topological space.  An \emph{open-set valuation} is a map
\(\nu:\mathsf{Prop}\to\mathcal P(X)\) whose values are open subsets of
\(X\), extended to formulas by

\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu(\bottom)&\defeq\varnothing,
 &\nu(A\land B)&\defeq\nu(A)\cap\nu(B),\\
 \nu(A\lor B)&\defeq\nu(A)\cup\nu(B),
 &\nu(A\to B)&\defeq
   \operatorname{int}_{X}
   \bigl((X\setminus\nu(A))\cup\nu(B)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus every formula denotes an open set.  The interior operation belongs to the
semantic algebra of opens; it is not a new object-language connective.  A
formula is valid under this semantics exactly when its value is \(X\) under
every open-set valuation.
\index{semantics!topological!intuitionistic}
\index{open-set valuation}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-topological-completeness
present_destinations.title: Topological completeness for IPL
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The theorems of IPL are exactly the formulas valid under all open-set
valuations on all topological spaces.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-bhk-reading
present_destinations.title: Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov explanatory reading
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The label \emph{BHK reading} is a metalinguistic abbreviation for the
following explanatory clauses, not the name of another derivability or
satisfaction relation.  A construction of \(A\land B\) is a pair of
constructions, one for each conjunct; a construction of \(A\lor B\) is a
tagged choice of a disjunct together with its construction; and a construction
of \(A\to B\) is a method transforming each construction of \(A\) into one of
\(B\).  There is no construction of \(\bottom\).  A construction of
\(\forall x\,A(x)\) is a method producing a construction of \(A(a)\) for every
admissible \(a\); a construction of \(\exists x\,A(x)\) supplies an admissible
witness together with a construction of its instance
\cite{Heyting1956,TroelstraVanDalen1988}.

The name is needed only to retrieve these six clauses as one explanatory
package.  It differs from both the formally recursive forcing relation in
Definition~\ref{sec:intuitionistic-logic-01} and the number-realizability relation in
Definition~\ref{def:p07-number-realizability}; the latter assigns natural
numbers and program indices according to an exact clause table.  This
distinction is used when reading the cited realizability theorem below.
\index{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}
\index{BHK|see{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}}

present_destinations.label: def:p07-number-realizability
present_destinations.title: Kleene number realizability
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Fix an acceptable numbering of the unary partial recursive functions, a
primitive-recursive pairing function, and projections \(\pi_0,\pi_1\).  For
a closed arithmetic formula \(\varphi\), the phrase
``the number \(e\) realizes \(\varphi\)'' is defined by structural recursion using
Table~\ref{tab:p07-number-realizability}.  It names a metalinguistic relation
between a natural number and an arithmetic formula; it is not the forcing or
satisfaction relation.  For formulas with numerical parameters, the cited
extension requires one index to realize all closed numeral instances
uniformly; that parameter clause is not silently identified with any one row
of the closed-formula table.  Pairing, program application, and definedness
are used by the soundness and ECT entries below \cite{Troelstra1998}.
\index{realizability!Kleene number}
\index{number realizability}

There is an effective transformation which, from an
\(\mathsf{HA}\)-derivation of a closed arithmetic sentence \(\varphi\), produces a

\hyperref[sheet:nj]{\texttt{sheet:nj}}, with no equality rules, nonlogical
axioms, or free parameters.  If it has a closed normal derivation, with no open
assumptions, of \(\exists x\,A(x)\), then its final inference supplies a closed
term \(t\) and a derivation of \(A(t)\).

present_destinations.label: def:p08-iqc-expanding-domain
present_destinations.title: Expanding-domain IQC model
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Here \emph{IQC} names the pure first-order logic of
\hyperref[sheet:lj]{\texttt{sheet:lj}} under the semantics now defined; the
name is needed to distinguish this setting from propositional IPL, but it does
not select a second rule sheet.  Fix an equality-free signature \(\Lang\).
An \emph{expanding-domain IQC model} consists of a nonempty preorder
\((W,\leq)\), a nonempty domain \(D_w\) for every \(w\in W\), and
interpretations at the worlds, subject to the following persistence data.
If \(w\leq u\), then \(D_w\subseteq D_u\); every constant denotes the same
element at later worlds; every function interpretation at \(u\) extends its
interpretation at \(w\); and every predicate extension at \(w\) is included in
its extension at \(u\).  These conditions make term values stable when an
assignment \(s:\mathsf{Var}\to D_w\) is viewed at a later world.

Atomic forcing uses the predicate interpretation at \(w\), and the
propositional clauses are those of
Definition~\ref{sec:intuitionistic-logic-01}.  The quantifier clauses are

\begin{itemize}
\item \(\mathcal M,w,s\forces\exists x\,A\) exactly when some
  \(a\in D_w\) has
  \(\mathcal M,w,s[x\mapsto a]\forces A\);
\item \(\mathcal M,w,s\forces\forall x\,A\) exactly when, for every
  \(u\geq w\) and every \(a\in D_u\),
  \(\mathcal M,u,s[x\mapsto a]\forces A\).
\end{itemize}

The expanding-domain hypothesis is load-bearing for persistence.  These
clauses define a satisfaction relation for IQC models, not modal
quantification and not a new object-language quantifier.
\index{intuitionistic first-order logic}
\index{Kripke model!expanding-domain intuitionistic}
\index{IQC|see{intuitionistic first-order logic}}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-iqc-completeness
present_destinations.title: IQC Kripke completeness
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every closed equality-free first-order formula \(A\),
\(\derives_{\mathsf{LJ}}A\) exactly when \(A\) is forced at every world under
every assignment in every expanding-domain IQC model of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-iqc-expanding-domain}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-iqc-constant-domain-principle
present_destinations.title: Constant-domain principle
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For a formula \(A\), a formula \(B(x)\), and a variable \(x\) not free in
\(A\), the \emph{constant-domain principle} is

\[
  \forall x\,(A\lor B(x))\to
  \bigl(A\lor\forall x\,B(x)\bigr).
\]

Its standing is an additional first-order intuitionistic schema.  It is not a
modal Barcan formula: the displayed quantifier is governed by the IQC clauses
above, and no modal operator occurs.
\index{constant-domain principle}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-iqc-constant-domain-boundary
present_destinations.title: Constant-domain validity boundary
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Every instance of the schema in
Definition~\ref{def:p08-iqc-constant-domain-principle} is valid when all
worlds have one common domain.  The schema can fail on expanding-domain IQC
models and is not a theorem of IQC.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-intermediate-logic
present_destinations.title: Intermediate propositional logic
present_destinations.declaration_text:
An \emph{intermediate propositional logic} is a set \(L\) of propositional
formulas which contains every IPL theorem, is contained in classical
propositional logic, and is closed under uniform substitution and modus
ponens.  This theorem-set notion is needed to compare strict extensions of
IPL without identifying them with arbitrary Kripke frame classes.  It differs
from an individual calculus presentation; the two instances below are used in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-intermediate-logics}.
\index{intermediate logic}
\index{superintuitionistic logic|see{intermediate logic}}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-intermediate-lattice
present_destinations.title: The complete lattice of intermediate logics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Order intermediate logics by theorem-set inclusion:
\[
 L\leq M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq M.
\]
For any family \(\{L_i:i\in I\}\), its meet is
\(\bigcap_{i\in I}L_i\).  Its join is the least intermediate logic containing
\(\bigcup_{i\in I}L_i\), equivalently the closure of that union under uniform
substitution and modus ponens.  With the empty-family conventions, the meet of
no logics is \(\mathsf{CPC}\) and the join of no logics is \(\mathsf{IPC}\).
Thus all intermediate logics form a complete lattice with bottom
\(\mathsf{IPC}\) and top \(\mathsf{CPC}\).

The lattice language is necessary because most intermediate logics are not
linearly ordered by inclusion.  It stands as a metalinguistic order on theorem
sets, not as a new object-language connective, and differs from the small
strict chain displayed below.  That chain is only a local subdiagram of the
full superintuitionistic lattice
\cite{ChagrovZakharyaschev1997}.
\index{intermediate logic!lattice}
\index{superintuitionistic logic!lattice}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-kc-profile
present_destinations.title: KC profile
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{KC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\(\neg A\lor\neg\neg A\).  It has the finite-model property; its standard
finite rooted-frame presentation uses a unique greatest world.  It does not
have the theorem-level disjunction property.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-lc-profile
present_destinations.title: G\"odel--Dummett logic profile
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{LC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\((A\to B)\lor(B\to A)\).  It is characterized by linearly ordered
intuitionistic frames, has the finite-model property, and does not have the
theorem-level disjunction property.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-intermediate-variety-correspondence
present_destinations.title: The lattice correspondence for intermediate logics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The assignments \(L\mapsto\mathsf V(L)\) and
\(\mathcal V\mapsto\operatorname{Log}(\mathcal V)\) are mutually
inverse order-reversing bijections between intermediate logics and
the interval of subvarieties
\[
 \mathsf{BA}\subseteq\mathcal V\subseteq\mathsf{HA}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \operatorname{Log}(\mathsf V(L))=L,\qquad
 \mathsf V(\operatorname{Log}(\mathcal V))=\mathcal V.
\]
The endpoints correspond as
\[
 \mathsf V(\mathsf{IPC})=\mathsf{HA},\qquad
 \mathsf V(\mathsf{CPL})=\mathsf{BA},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Log}(\mathsf{HA})=\mathsf{IPC},\quad
 \operatorname{Log}(\mathsf{BA})=\mathsf{CPL}.
\]
These are complete lattices.  On the logic side, nonempty meets are
intersections and joins are the least MP- and substitution-closed
extensions of IPC containing the union.  The empty meet is CPL and
the empty join is IPC.
On the variety side, nonempty meets are intersections and joins are
the least subvarieties containing \(\mathsf{BA}\) and the union.
The empty meet is \(\mathsf{HA}\) and the empty join is \(\mathsf{BA}\).
The correspondence interchanges all these meets and joins.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices
present_destinations.title: Cignoli's finite chain and H\'ajek's standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(n\geq2\), Cignoli, D'Ottaviano, and Mundici write the finite
MV-chain itself as
\[
 \text{\L}_n=\left\{0,\frac1{n-1},\frac2{n-1},\ldots,1\right\}.
\]
The \(n\)-valued Lukasiewicz system uses this value algebra, designated set
\(D=\{1\}\), and the operations
\[
  \neg x=1-x,
  \qquad
  x\Rightarrow y=\min(1,1-x+y).
\]
H\'ajek writes the standard infinite-valued logic as \(\text{\L}\); its
standard value algebra is \([0,1]\).  Its derived strong conjunction is
\(x\mathbin{\ast_{\text{\L}}}y=\max(0,x+y-1)\); weak conjunction and
disjunction are minimum and maximum.  These are H\'ajek's source symbols:
\(\Rightarrow\) is typed here as the truth-function implication and
\(\ast_{\text{\L}}\) as the Lukasiewicz t-norm.  A finite system based on
\(\text{\L}_n\) uses
the generic finite-matrix sheet; the standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics does not
\cite{Lukasiewicz1920,LukasiewiczTarski1930,Hajek1998,
  CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.
\index{Lukasiewicz logic}
\index{many-valued logic!Lukasiewicz}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-finite-lukasiewicz-tableau
present_destinations.title: Finite-chain tableau adequacy and decision
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every fixed \(n\geq2\), instantiate
\hyperref[sheet:tableaux-matrix]{\texttt{sheet:tableaux-matrix}} with
\(\text{\L}_n\), designated set \(\{1\}\), and the operations of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices}.  A finite-premise sequent is
valid in that matrix exactly when every corresponding labelled tableau closes;
the exhaustive expansion terminates and decides consequence.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-lukasiewicz-completeness
present_destinations.title: Lukasiewicz completeness
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For the exact calculus on
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite}}, in the language of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices}:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item a formula is a theorem iff every valuation in the standard
        \([0,1]\)-matrix gives it value \(1\);
  \item for a finite premise set, syntactic consequence agrees with preservation
        of value \(1\) in that standard matrix.
\end{enumerate}
These clauses do not license arbitrary-premise strong completeness for the
single standard matrix.  The exact definition of the corresponding algebraic
semantics and its arbitrary-premise completeness theorem are treated in
Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}; no algebra class is silently introduced
here \cite{CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-mcnaughton
present_destinations.title: McNaughton's theorem
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A function \(g:[0,1]^m\to[0,1]\) is the truth function of an
\(m\)-variable infinite-valued Lukasiewicz formula iff \(g\) is continuous and
piecewise linear with integer coefficients on every linear piece.  The theorem
does not represent arbitrary continuous functions, and it is not an
arbitrary-premise completeness statement.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-tnorm-residuum
present_destinations.title: T-norm and residuum
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{t-norm} is a commutative, associative, coordinatewise monotone
operation \(\ast:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\) with unit \(1\).  If \(\ast\) is
left-continuous, its \emph{residuum} is
\[
  x\Rightarrow y
  =\sup\{z\in[0,1]:x\ast z\leq y\}.
\]
The t-norm interprets strong conjunction, whereas lattice conjunction remains
minimum; the residuum is a semantic operation interpreting object-language
implication.  The source uses the plain glyph \(\Rightarrow\); its numeric
operands type it as a residuum rather than a sequent arrow.  These distinctions
are needed in every row of Table~\ref{tab:p08-tnorm-logics}
\cite{Hajek1998,CintulaHajekNoguera2011}.
\index{t-norm}
\index{residuum!t-norm}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-tnorm-completeness
present_destinations.title: Propositional t-norm completeness survey
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) lie in the language of the indicated sheet, and let
standard consequence mean preservation of the value \(1\).  If \(\Gamma\) is
finite, then for each
\[
 S\in\{\mathrm{MTL},\mathrm{BL},\mathsf L_{\infty},G,\Pi\},
\]
\(\Gamma\derives_S A\) exactly when every standard \(S\)-evaluation assigning
value \(1\) to every member of \(\Gamma\) assigns value \(1\) to \(A\).
For MTL the standard class ranges over all left-continuous t-norms; for BL it
ranges over all continuous t-norms; the remaining three rows use their single
displayed standard chain.  The restriction that \(\Gamma\) be finite may be
dropped for MTL and \(G\), but not for BL, \(\mathsf L_{\infty}\), or
\(\Pi\).  Arbitrary-premise algebraic completeness uses the corresponding
MTL-, BL-, MV-, G\"odel-, or Product-algebra class, as summarized in the table
and defined in Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}
\cite{Hajek1998,CignoliEstevaGodoTorrens2000,JeneiMontagna2002}.

present_destinations.label: def:p10-mv-algebra
present_destinations.title: MV-algebra
present_destinations.declaration_text:
An MV-algebra is a nonempty algebra \((A,\oplus,\neg,0)\) satisfying, for all
\(x,y,z\in A\),
\[
\begin{gathered}
x\oplus(y\oplus z)=(x\oplus y)\oplus z,\qquad
x\oplus y=y\oplus x,\qquad x\oplus0=x,\\
\neg\neg x=x,\qquad x\oplus\neg0=\neg0,\\
\neg(\neg x\oplus y)\oplus y
=\neg(\neg y\oplus x)\oplus x.
\end{gathered}
\]
Put \(1=\neg0\), define \(x\to y=\neg x\oplus y\), put
\(x\le y\) iff \(x\to y=1\), and
\(x\odot y=\neg(\neg x\oplus\neg y)\). The standard algebra on \([0,1]\) has
\(x\oplus y=\min(1,x+y)\) and \(\neg x=1-x\). The name is needed to identify
the exact algebraic semantics of infinite-valued \L{}ukasiewicz logic rather
than an arbitrary many-valued algebra. It stands as an equational class,
differs through the Chang identities and truncated addition, and is used in
standard completeness and the ordered-group correspondence.
\index{MV-algebra}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-post-n-valued
present_destinations.title: Post's cyclic \(n\)-valued matrices
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(V_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), designate \(n-1\), put
\(\sim x=x+1\pmod n\), and put \(x\vee y=\max(x,y)\) in the displayed linear
order. The name is needed to fix this cyclic-negation/max family rather than
every logic studied in Post's general classification. It stands as a family of
finite matrices, differs from \L{}ukasiewicz chains because its negation is
cyclic rather than involutive, and is used in the decidability and functional-
generation statement \cite{Post1921}.
\index{Post many-valued logic}\index{cyclic negation}

present_destinations.declaration_text:
For each fixed \(n\), validity and finite-premise consequence in the matrix of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-post-n-valued} are decidable by exhaustive valuation.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-post-matrix
present_destinations.title: Post finite-valued generation boundary
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The displayed Post operations generate the truth functions of the corresponding
finite-valued calculus as established in the cited presentation.  This does
not identify different \(n\), and it does not transfer the two-valued clone
classification of \cite{Post1941} without a separate translation.

present_destinations.label: annex:p8.post.1
present_destinations.title: Decision for each fixed Post matrix
present_destinations.declaration_text:
\begin{proof}
For a finite input using \(m\) propositional variables, enumerate the
\(n^m\) valuations into \(V_n\), evaluate every formula recursively under the
displayed cyclic negation and maximum operation, and reject exactly when a
valuation designates all premises but not the conclusion.  The finite search
terminates and decides the fixed-matrix consequence relation.
\end{proof}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-fde-matrix
present_destinations.title: The FDE support-pair matrix
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let
\[
 \mathrm{BD}=\{(0,1),(0,0),(1,1),(1,0)\}
 =\{f,n,b,t\},
\]
in the displayed order.  For a value \(x=(x^+,x^-)\), the coordinates are its
positive and negative support indicators.  They are needed because a single
linear scale cannot distinguish neither support from both support.  For
\(x=(x^+,x^-)\) and \(y=(y^+,y^-)\), put
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \neg x&=(x^-,x^+),\\
 x\land y&=(x^+\land y^+,\ x^-\lor y^-),\\
 x\lor y&=(x^+\lor y^+,\ x^-\land y^-),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the coordinate operations are Boolean.  Designate
\(\{b,t\}\), exactly the values with positive support.
This finite matrix defines the displayed propositional first-degree-entailment
semantics \cite{Dunn1976,Belnap1977,OmoriWansing2017}.
\index{first-degree entailment}
\index{FDE}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-fde-orders
present_destinations.title: Orders on the BD algebra
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(x,y\in\mathrm{BD}\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 x\leq_t y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ y^-\leq x^-,\\
 x\leq_k y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ x^-\leq y^-.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first compares truth support against falsity support; the second compares
total information componentwise.  They are two relations on the same values,
not two consequence relations.  Their nonredundancy is visible at once:
\(n\) and \(b\) are incomparable in the truth order, whereas
they are respectively bottom and top in the information order.  A
\emph{bilattice} is an algebraic structure whose carrier bears two lattice
orders.  The displayed carrier qualifies: truth-order meet and join are
\((\min(x^+,y^+),\max(x^-,y^-))\) and
\((\max(x^+,y^+),\min(x^-,y^-))\), while information-order meet and join take
coordinatewise minima and maxima.  Thus ``bilattice'' records both lattice
orders at once and cannot be replaced by either order alone.  This distinction
is used by the FDE card.
\index{bilattice}
\index{truth order}
\index{information order}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-k3-lp-facts
present_destinations.title: K3--LP theorem sets and dual consequence
present_destinations.declaration_text:
In the fixed constant-free \(\neg,\land,\lor\)-language:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathbf K_3\) has no tautologies;
  \item the LP tautologies are exactly the classical tautologies;
  \item for finite formula sets \(\Gamma,\Delta\), if
        \(\Gamma\entails_S\Delta\) means that every valuation designating all
        members of \(\Gamma\) designates at least one member of \(\Delta\),
        then
        \[
          \Gamma\entails_{\mathbf K_3}\Delta
          \quad\text{ iff }\quad
          \neg\Delta\entails_{\mathsf{LP}}\neg\Gamma,
        \]
        where negation acts memberwise on each finite set.
\end{enumerate}
The third clause is the registered K3--LP duality.  It is not an unqualified
single-conclusion equivalence \cite{Priest1979,OmoriWansing2017}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-weak-kleene-matrix
present_destinations.title: Weak Kleene matrix
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The \emph{weak Kleene matrix} has values
\(\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\), designates only \(1\), fixes
\(\neg\tfrac12=\tfrac12\), and makes \(\tfrac12\) infectious for every
nonunary classical connective: if any immediate argument has that value, so
does the compound; otherwise the operation is classical.  Infectiousness is
an exact operation clause, not the informal claim that a sentence is
meaningless.  This definition is used in Table~\ref{tab:p08-many-valued-matrices}
and nowhere as a substitute for Bochvar's richer external language
\cite{Kleene1952}.
\index{weak Kleene logic}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-bochvar-external
present_destinations.title: Bochvar's external three-valued language
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Extend the weak-Kleene matrix of Definition~\ref{def:p08-weak-kleene-matrix}
by unary assertion operators
\[
 J_T(x)=\begin{cases}1&x=1\\0&x\ne1,\end{cases}\quad
 J_F(x)=\begin{cases}1&x=0\\0&x\ne0,\end{cases}\quad
 J_N(x)=\begin{cases}1&x=\tfrac12\\0&x\ne\tfrac12.\end{cases}
\]
Internal connectives remain infectious; the external operators return only
classical values. The external-language name is necessary because the weak
Kleene internal matrix alone cannot assert that a formula is meaningful,
true, false, or nonsensical. It stands as an expanded truth-functional
language, differs through the three classical-valued assertions, and is used
by the finite-matrix tableau and adequacy statement
\cite{Bochvar1938English1981}.
\index{Bochvar logic}\index{external assertion operator}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-bochvar-tableau
present_destinations.title: Finite-matrix adequacy for the Bochvar language
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Instantiate \texttt{sheet:tableaux-matrix} with the three values, designated
set \(\{1\}\), infectious internal operations, and the displayed assertion
tables. A formula is valid exactly when every fully expanded tableau for its
nondesignated root closes. This is ordinary finite truth-table adequacy for the
fixed expanded matrix, not an adequacy claim for a different Bochvar calculus
or for partial valuations.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-supervaluation
present_destinations.title: Fine specification spaces and supertruth
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Following Fine's presentation, a \emph{specification space} is a partially
ordered collection of specification-points, where the order records extension
of information.  A \emph{base-point} is the specification-point being
evaluated.  A point above it is a \emph{completion} when it gives a complete
classical specification, and it is \emph{admissible} when it satisfies the
primitive admissibility constraints of that specification space.  The
base-point is \emph{completeable} when at least one complete admissible point
extends it.

At a completeable base-point, a formula is \emph{supertrue} iff it is true at
every complete admissible specification extending that point,
\emph{superfalse} iff it is false at every such specification, and
\emph{indeterminate} otherwise.  Specification-points and admissibility are
metalinguistic semantic data, not matrix truth values.  The extension order is
needed to keep only completions of the base information, while admissibility
can further restrict those completions; neither condition subsumes the other.
This distinction is used in the preservation theorem and example below
\cite{Fine1975}.
\index{supervaluation}
\index{admissible precisification}
\index{supertruth}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-supervaluation-classical
present_destinations.title: Classical tautologies under supervaluation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Every classical tautology is supertrue at every completeable base-point.  The
converse holds when every complete classical specification is an admissible
completion of the base-point, but need not hold when primitive admissibility
restricts its completions.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-supervaluation-gap
present_destinations.title: Supertruth with an indeterminate atom
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Suppose two complete admissible specifications extending one base-point
disagree about \(p\).  Then \(p\) is neither supertrue nor superfalse, but every
such specification makes
\(p\lor\neg p\) true, so that compound is supertrue.  Supertruth therefore is
not a truth-functional third value assigned compositionally from the three
supervaluation statuses of immediate constituents.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-cll-language
present_destinations.title: CLL formulas and linear negation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The cited one-sided CLL presentation has paired atoms
\(p,p^\perp\), multiplicative units \(\mathbf 1,\bot\), additive units
\(\top,0\), and are closed under
\(\otimes,\bindnasrepma,\mathbin{\&},\oplus,!,?\).  Formula-level
\emph{linear negation} is the involution fixed on atoms and by
\[
\begin{gathered}
 (A\otimes B)^\perp=A^\perp\bindnasrepma B^\perp,
 \qquad
 (A\bindnasrepma B)^\perp=A^\perp\otimes B^\perp,\\
 \mathbf 1^\perp=\bot,\quad \bot^\perp=\mathbf 1,\qquad
 (A\mathbin{\&}B)^\perp=A^\perp\oplus B^\perp,\\
 (A\oplus B)^\perp=A^\perp\mathbin{\&}B^\perp,
 \qquad \top^\perp=0,\quad 0^\perp=\top,\\
 (!A)^\perp=?A^\perp,\qquad(?A)^\perp=!A^\perp.
\end{gathered}
\]
This name is necessary to distinguish an operation on formulas from Routley
star and from phase orthogonality on sets.  Its standing is a syntactic De
Morgan operation, not ordinary object-language falsum; it differs from
primitive negation in the relevance language and is used by the one-sided
sheet, connective table, and phase interpretation.  Linear implication is the
defined connective \(A\multimap B\defeq A^\perp\bindnasrepma B\).
\index{linear negation}
\index{classical linear logic}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-focusing-polarity
present_destinations.title: Andreoli focusing polarity
present_destinations.declaration_text:
In Andreoli's one-sided focusing convention used for the displayed CLL
presentation, a formula constructor is
\emph{positive} when its introduction is assigned to a synchronous focused
phase, and \emph{negative} when its introduction is assigned to an
asynchronous phase whose available introduction is invertible.  The positive
nullary connective \(0\) has no introduction rule, so the first clause does
not assert that every positive constructor supplies an applicable rule.  Each
atom receives a declared polarity, and its formal linear negation receives the
opposite polarity.  This is a metalinguistic classification used to schedule
focused proof search, not an object-language connective or a semantic truth
value.  The name is necessary to distinguish the synchronous/asynchronous
proof-search discipline from De Morgan duality and from positive or negative
truth; those classifications do not determine one another.  Table
\ref{tab:p08-linear-connectives} uses the distinction to record the source
constructor classes \cite{Andreoli1992}.
\index{focusing polarity}

present_destinations.declaration_text:
Every sequent derivable on \hyperref[sheet:cll-one-sided]{the registered

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-linear-decision-boundaries
present_destinations.title: Linear-logic decision boundaries
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Full propositional linear logic with exponentials is undecidable.  Its
fragment with multiplicatives and additives but no exponentials is
PSPACE-complete, while the multiplicative fragment is NP-complete.  These are
three distinct input languages and do not transfer a decision result to the
source's unnamed four-rule bang extension.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-phase-space
present_destinations.title: Full-CLL phase semantics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{phase space}, in Girard's notation, is a pair \((M,\perp)\), where
\(M\) is a commutative monoid written multiplicatively, with unit \(1\), and
\(\perp\subseteq M\) is the \emph{pole}.  For \(X,Y\subseteq M\), define the
phase-subset residual and phase orthogonal by
\[
 X\multimap Y
 =\{m\in M:\forall x\in X\
      (mx\in Y)\},
 \qquad
 X^{\perp}
 =X\multimap\perp.
\]
A \emph{fact} is a subset \(X\subseteq M\) with
\(X=X^{\perp\perp}\).  Here the source uses the same glyph
\({}^{\perp}\) for formula negation and subset orthogonality; the operand type
makes the two roles exact.  These names are needed
to distinguish the semantic model, its designated orthogonality test, and its
closed semantic values from formula-level linear negation.  Here \(\perp\) is
locally typed as a subset of \(M\), not as the formula-level par unit.  Their standing is
semantic: the residual is a typed operation on phase subsets, the pole is a
subset of phases, and a fact is a closed subset, not a formula or a proof
object.  The phase residual differs from formula-level \(\multimap\) by its
subset operands, and is used to define phase orthogonality.  The distinctions
are used in every interpretation clause and in
Theorem~\ref{thm:p08-phase-adequacy}.

Interpret atoms as facts.  Following Girard, write \(A^*\) for the fact
interpreting formula \(A\), and use the connective glyphs themselves for the
corresponding operations on facts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 X\otimes Y&=\{xy:
                     x\in X, y\in Y\}^{\perp\perp},
 &X\bindnasrepma Y&=(X^\perp\otimes Y^\perp)^\perp,\\
 (\mathbf 1)^*&=\{1\}^{\perp\perp},
 &\bot^*&=\{1\}^{\perp},\\
 X\mathbin{\&}Y&=X\cap Y,
 &X\oplus Y&=(X\cup Y)^{\perp\perp},\\
 \top^*&=M,
 &0^*&=\varnothing^{\perp\perp}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the exponentials define the idempotent phase set
\[
 I=\{m\in\{1\}^{\perp\perp}:mm=m\},
\]
and set
\[
 !X=(X\cap I)^{\perp\perp},
 \qquad
 ?X=(X^\perp\cap I)^\perp.
\]
The set \(I\) is required for the cited phase interpretation; omitting
it would define only an exponential-free phase semantics.  A formula \(A\) is
\emph{phase-valid} iff \(1\in A^*\) in every such interpretation.  This
validity differs from membership in one phase
model and is the notion used in the next theorem \cite{Girard1995}.
\index{phase semantics}
\index{fact!linear logic}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-phase-adequacy
present_destinations.title: Phase soundness and completeness
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For every formula \(A\) in the displayed full propositional CLL language,
\[
 \derives_{\mathsf{CLL}}A
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 1\in A^*
 \text{ in every displayed phase interpretation}.
\]
The theorem is formula theoremhood.  The exponential clauses and idempotent
phase set in Definition~\ref{def:p08-phase-space} are part of its hypotheses;
an MALL-only interpretation may not be advertised as this full result.

present_destinations.declaration_text:
Girard's coherence-space semantics and proof nets are entry points in the
original linear-logic development \cite{Girard1987}.  The recorded
\hyperref[def:p07-proof-nets-goi-boundary]{Part-7 proof-net and geometry-of-interaction
boundary} governs the scope: no proof-net correctness criterion,
sequentialization theorem, net-based cut elimination, or
geometry-of-interaction execution model is developed.  Quantum logic,
adaptive logics, and formal argumentation are also outside this chapter's
technical scope.  For the orthomodular-lattice program of quantum logic see
\textcite{BirkhoffVonNeumann1936}; for the dynamic marking strategy of adaptive
logics see \textcite{Batens2007}; and for abstract argumentation frameworks and
their extension semantics see \textcite{Dung1995}.  These are source-specific
navigation pointers, not imported definitions or theorem claims.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-generalized-sequent-frameworks
present_destinations.title: Generalized sequent frameworks
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The following four names are required because they alter different parts of
a derivation object; calling all of them ``nonstandard sequents'' would erase
the distinction needed to choose a rule sheet.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A \emph{hypersequent} is a finite sequence or multiset of sequents,
        with a separately declared external separator and separately declared
        external structural rules.
  \item A \emph{labelled sequent} contains labelled formulas such as
        \(w{:}\varphi\) and relational atoms such as \(wRv\), so a selected
        Kripke frame relation occurs inside the derivation language.
  \item A \emph{display calculus} has a structural language and reversible
        display postulates with the display property: any chosen substructure
        of a sequent can be made the entire antecedent or entire consequent of
        a structurally equivalent sequent.
  \item A \emph{deep-inference calculus} permits a rule instance inside an
        arbitrary formula or structure context, rather than only at its root.
\end{enumerate}
Their standing is architectural: each describes a class of derivation
objects, not a single logic or an adequacy theorem.  They are nonredundant
  respectively because they add external components, semantic labels, a
  residuated structural language, or non-root rule application.  The comparison
  table and the selected system-specific examples below use exactly these four
  distinctions
  \cite{Avron1996,Negri2005,Belnap1982,Wansing1994,Guglielmi2007,Stouppa2007}.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-worked-derivation-boundary
present_destinations.title: A worked derivation is not adequacy
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Even after a system-specific sheet exists, one complete derivation proves only
that its endformula is derivable.  Soundness, completeness, cut admissibility,
and correspondence with a frame class require separate status-bearing
results.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-gs5-derivation
present_destinations.title: Avron GS5 derives axiom 5
present_destinations.declaration_text:
On \hyperref[sheet:gs5-avron]{\texttt{sheet:gs5-avron}}, start with
\(\Box p\Rightarrow\Box p\). Lifted negation-left gives
\(\Box p,\neg\Box p\Rightarrow\). Modalized Splitting gives
\[
 \Box p\Rightarrow\ \mid\ \neg\Box p\Rightarrow.
\]
Lifted negation-right in the first component yields
\(\Rightarrow\neg\Box p\mid\neg\Box p\Rightarrow\), and Box-R yields
\(\Rightarrow\Box\neg\Box p\mid\neg\Box p\Rightarrow\).
Internal weakening makes both components
\(\neg\Box p\Rightarrow\Box\neg\Box p\); external contraction merges them,
and implication-right concludes
\(\Rightarrow\neg\Box p\to\Box\neg\Box p\). Every structural step is on the
sheet, and the lifted propositional rules are those of classical LK
\cite{Avron1996}.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-labelled-k-derivation
present_destinations.title: Negri labelled \(K\) derives the K axiom
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Work backward on
\(\Rightarrow x:\Box(A\to B)\to(\Box A\to\Box B)\) using
\hyperref[sheet:labelled-k-negri]{\texttt{sheet:labelled-k-negri}}. Two
Implication-R steps reduce the goal to
\(x:\Box(A\to B),x:\Box A\Rightarrow x:\Box B\). Box-R introduces a fresh
\(y\) and relational atom \(xRy\). Two Box-L steps expose
\(y:A\to B\) and \(y:A\). Implication-L closes the remaining goal from the
identity sequents \(y:A\Rightarrow y:A\) and
\(y:B\Rightarrow y:B\). The freshness of \(y\) is the only eigenlabel
condition; no reflexivity or transitivity rule is used, so the derivation is in
basic \(K\) \cite{Negri2005}.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-display-k-derivation
present_destinations.title: A complete modal-display cycle in Wansing's calculus
present_destinations.declaration_text:
On \hyperref[sheet:display-k-wansing]{\texttt{sheet:display-k-wansing}}, the
identity \(A\Rightarrow A\) first gives
\(\Box A\Rightarrow\bullet A\) by Box-L.  Apply Modal Display in its declared
reverse direction to obtain
\(\bullet\Box A\Rightarrow A\), then apply Box-R:
\[
 A\Rightarrow A
 \;\overset{\Box L}{\Longrightarrow}\;
 \Box A\Rightarrow\bullet A
 \;\overset{\text{Modal Display}^{-1}}{\Longrightarrow}\;
 \bullet\Box A\Rightarrow A
 \;\overset{\Box R}{\Longrightarrow}\;
 \Box A\Rightarrow\Box A.
\]
Every intermediate sequent is therefore reconstructible from the three named
rows of the printed sheet.  The example exhibits the structural modal operator
on both sides of a display sequent; it is not offered as a derivation of the K
axiom or as an adequacy proof \cite{Wansing1994}.

present_destinations.label: def:p07-deep-s5-derivation
present_destinations.title: Stouppa deep inference derives axiom B
present_destinations.declaration_text:
On \hyperref[sheet:deep-s5-stouppa]{\texttt{sheet:deep-s5-stouppa}}, apply
i-down to \(\mathsf{tt}\) with structure \(\Diamond\Box a\), obtaining
\([\Diamond\Box a,\Box\Diamond\bar a]\). Apply 5-down inside the left
disjunct to obtain \([\Box a,\Box\Diamond\bar a]\), then t-down there to obtain
\([a,\Box\Diamond\bar a]\). With \(a=\neg p\), this is
\(p\to\Box\Diamond p\), axiom B. Both modal rules act strictly below the outer
disjunction, which is the promised deep-inference use \cite{Stouppa2007}.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-pointed-rm-frame
present_destinations.title: Matched relevance frames
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{pointed Routley--Meyer frame} is
\(\mathfrak F=(K,R,0,{*})\), with nonempty \(K\), distinguished
\(0\in K\), ternary \(R\), and star on \(K\).  Define
\(a\leq b\) iff \(R(0,a,b)\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R^2(ab)cd &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,c,d)),\\
 R^2a(bc)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(b,c,x)\land R(a,x,d)),\\
 R^2b(ac)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,c,x)\land R(b,x,d)),\\
 R^2abbc &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,b,c)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are metalinguistic abbreviations for composite ternary conditions, not
new accessibility relations.

The cited modular presentation uses the base conditions
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{B1}:&\ a\leq a,\\
 \mathrm{B2}:&\ a\leq b\land b\leq c\text{ implies }a\leq c,\\
 \mathrm{B3}:&\ a'\leq a\land R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(a',b,c),\\
 \mathrm{B4}:&\ a^{**}=a,\\
 \mathrm{B5}:&\ a\leq b\text{ implies }b^*\leq a^*.
\end{align*}
The labels are metalinguistic names for the five displayed frame conditions,
not object-language schemas.  Its \(\mathbf E\)-frames satisfy
B1--B5 and, universally,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{E3}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2a(bc)d,\qquad
 \mathrm{E4}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2b(ac)d,\\
 \mathrm{E5}:\ R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R^2abbc,\qquad
 \mathrm{E6}:\ R(a,0,a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Its \(\mathbf R\)-frames are those \(\mathbf E\)-frames also
satisfying \(\mathrm{R7}: R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(b,a,c)\).  Its
\(\mathbf{RM}\)-frames additionally satisfy
\(\mathrm{M}: 0\leq a\) or \(0\leq a^*\), for every \(a\).  A valuation is
hereditary along \(\leq\), and the satisfaction clauses are those of
Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}; formula validity is truth at the
distinguished point \(0\).  These are semantic frame classes matched to the
three exact sheets, not the broad class above
\cite{RoutleyMeyer1973,DunnRestall2002}.  A different direct R-frame package
uses period two together with an inversion condition; it is not silently
combined with this modular B1--B5/E3--E6/R7/M presentation.
\index{pointed Routley--Meyer frame}

present_destinations.label: entry:p08-relevance-r
present_destinations.title: Relevant implication \(\mathbf R\)

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-relevance-adequacy
present_destinations.title: Relevance theoremhood adequacy
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(X\in\{\mathbf E,\mathbf R,\mathbf{RM}\}\), let the calculus and
pointed frame class be exactly those fixed by the corresponding registry sheet
and Definition~\ref{def:p08-pointed-rm-frame}.  Then
\[
 \derives_X A\quad\text{ iff }\quad\entails_X A
\]
for formula theoremhood.  The statement does not identify theoremhood with an
arbitrary-premise relevant consequence relation and does not apply to the
broad frames of Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-relevance-variable-sharing
present_destinations.title: Variable sharing for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be constant-free formulas.  If
\(\derives_{\mathbf E} A\to B\) or
\(\derives_{\mathbf R} A\to B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have a propositional
variable in common.  This is a theoremhood property of implications, not an
arbitrary-premise consequence theorem and not a sufficient definition of
relevance.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-gamma-admissibility
present_destinations.title: Gamma admissibility for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(X\in\{\mathbf E,\mathbf R\}\), if
\(\derives_X A\) and \(\derives_X\neg A\lor B\), then
\(\derives_X B\).  Gamma is not added to either registry sheet: the theorem
says that the metarule preserves theoremhood.  No theory-uniform
\(\mathbf{RM}\) generalization is asserted here.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-lambek-semantics
present_destinations.title: Lambek L and its algebra
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Lambek's \emph{associative calculus \(\mathsf L\)} has formulas
generated from atoms by product \(A\mathbin{\cdot}B\), left division
\(A\backslash B\), and right division \(B/A\).  Antecedents are finite
nonempty ordered sequences; the calculus has no exchange, weakening,
contraction, empty antecedent, or multiplicative unit.  This exact name is
necessary to distinguish \(\mathsf L\) from \(\mathsf L^*\), which permits
empty antecedents, and from \(\mathsf L_1\), which adds a unit.  Its standing
is the proof system on \hyperref[sheet:lambek-l]{the Lambek sheet}, and the
distinction is used in its card and complexity statement.

A \emph{residuated semigroup} is a partially ordered semigroup
\((U,\mathbin{\cdot},\leq)\) with residuals satisfying
\[
 a\mathbin{\cdot}b\leq c
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 b\leq a\backslash c
 \quad\text{ iff }\quad
 a\leq c/b.
\]
Its standing is algebraic semantics, not syntax; unlike the IMLL algebra it
need not be commutative or have a unit.  A sequent
\(A_1,\ldots,A_n\Rightarrow B\) is valid iff
\(v(A_1)\mathbin{\cdot}\cdots\mathbin{\cdot}v(A_n)\leq v(B)\) under every
valuation in every such semigroup \cite{Lambek1958,Buszkowski2010}.
\index{Lambek calculus}

present_destinations.label: def:p10-residuated-lattice
present_destinations.title: Residuated lattice
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A residuated lattice is a lattice-ordered monoid
\((A,\wedge,\vee,\otimes,1)\) with residuals satisfying
\[
 a\otimes b\le c
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 b\le a\backslash c
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 a\le c/b.
\]
The two residuals are necessary when exchange is absent; in a commutative
algebra they coincide. This stands as the algebraic semantics of Full
Lambek-style calculi, differs from a Heyting algebra by separating monoidal
product from lattice meet, and is used to track weakening, contraction, and
exchange as algebraic equations \cite{OnoKomori1985,
GalatosJipsenKowalskiOno2007}.
\index{residuated lattice}\index{FL-algebra}
