present_destinations.label: def:p08-default-theory
present_destinations.title: Reiter default theory
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A default is written
\(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\): prerequisite \(\alpha\),
justifications \(\beta_i\), and conclusion \(\gamma\). A default theory
\((W,D)\) has facts \(W\) and defaults \(D\).  For a candidate theory \(E\),
let \(\Gamma_E\) be the least set \(U\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(W\subseteq U\);
  \item \(U=\operatorname{Th}(U)\); and
  \item if
    \(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\in D\),
    \(\alpha\in U\), and \(\neg\beta_i\notin E\) for every \(i\), then
    \(\gamma\in U\).
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, start with \(U_0=\operatorname{Th}(W)\), close each successor
stage under classical consequence after adding every conclusion whose
prerequisite is in the current stage and whose justifications are consistent
with \(E\), and take the union of the stages.  The candidate \(E\) is a
\emph{Reiter extension} exactly when \(E=\Gamma_E\).

The term is needed because applicability tests justifications against the
candidate \(E\), while prerequisite support is grounded in the least set
\(\Gamma_E\).  It stands as a theory-plus-fixed-point semantics, differs from
the circular condition that tests prerequisites directly in \(E\), and is used
to explain absent, multiple, credulous, and skeptical conclusions
\cite{Reiter1980}.
\index{default logic}\index{default extension}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-circumscription
present_destinations.title: Predicate circumscription
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Write the first-order theory as \(T(\bar P,\bar Q,\bar Z)\), where \(\bar P\)
is minimized, \(\bar Q\) is fixed, and \(\bar Z\) may vary.  For predicate
tuples of matching arities, let \(\bar P'\leq\bar P\) abbreviate the
componentwise universal closures of \(P'_i(\bar x)\to P_i(\bar x)\).
Circumscription is the second-order sentence
\[
 T(\bar P,\bar Q,\bar Z)\land
 \forall\bar P'\forall\bar Z'
 \Bigl((T(\bar P',\bar Q,\bar Z')\land\bar P'\leq\bar P)
       \to\bar P\leq\bar P'\Bigr).
\]
Thus no model with the same fixed \(\bar Q\) can make the minimized predicates
strictly smaller while adjusting only the declared varying predicates.  The
name is necessary because the minimized, fixed, and varying tuples determine
different policies.  It stands as a model-minimization transformation,
differs from syntactic default application, and is used to formalize minimal
abnormality \cite{McCarthy1980}.
\index{circumscription}\index{predicate minimization}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-autoepistemic-expansion
present_destinations.title: Stable expansion in autoepistemic logic
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(T\) be a theory in the Boolean language closed under the belief operator
\(L\).  Write \(\operatorname{Th}\) for ordinary classical propositional
closure over that language: modal-prefixed subformulas are formulas, but this
closure adds no modal axiom or necessitation rule.  A \emph{stable expansion}
is a theory \(E\) satisfying
\[
 E=\operatorname{Th}
 \bigl(T\cup\{LA:A\in E\}\cup\{\neg LA:A\notin E\}\bigr).
\]
The name is necessary because the agent's positive and negative introspective
assumptions are determined by the candidate theory itself.  It names a fixed
point, not a Reiter default extension: default prerequisites are grounded
through \(\Gamma_E\), whereas the belief and nonbelief assumptions here are
closed as one expansion.  Its classical closure also differs from simply
declaring \(L\) to be a KD45 modality; the comparison table uses this exact
distinction \cite{Moore1985}.
\index{autoepistemic logic}\index{stable expansion!autoepistemic}

present_destinations.title: AGM revision and contraction
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Let \(K\) be a deductively closed classical belief set. A revision operation
\(K*A\) maps a formula input to a deductively closed belief set.  Write
\(K+A=\operatorname{Th}(K\cup\{A\})\) for expansion.  A contraction operation
\(K-A\) maps \(A\) to a deductively closed subset of \(K\) intended no longer
to imply \(A\), except when \(A\) is a tautology.  The revision and contraction
postulates are displayed in
Tables~\ref{tab:p08-agm-postulates}
and~\ref{tab:p08-agm-contraction-postulates}.  In particular, revision
Inclusion is unconditional, whereas the consistency hypothesis belongs to
Vacuity.  These names are necessary to distinguish adding an input
consistently, removing commitment to it, and merely expanding by it.  They
stand as operations on belief sets, differ from nonmonotonic consequence by
taking an explicit prior state and input, and are used by the identities and
representation theorem below
\cite{AlchourronGardenforsMakinson1985}.
\index{AGM belief revision}\index{belief contraction}\index{belief update}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-agm-faithful-preorder
present_destinations.title: Faithful preorder for a belief set
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Fix a finite propositional signature and let \(\mathcal W\) be its valuations.
For a consistent belief set \(K\), a total preorder \(\preceq_K\) on
\(\mathcal W\) is \emph{faithful to \(K\)} exactly when all valuations
satisfying \(K\) are tied and every such valuation is strictly preferred to
every valuation that does not satisfy \(K\).  Write
\(\min([A],\preceq_K)\) for the \(\preceq_K\)-minimal \(A\)-valuations and
\(\operatorname{Th}(X)\) for the formulas true at every member of \(X\).

The qualifier is necessary because an arbitrary total preorder need not
preserve the prior beliefs when they are consistent with the input.  It names
semantic data assigned to \(K\), not another revision operation, and differs
from the preferential models of Definition~\ref{def:p08-preferential-model}
because it orders all classical valuations relative to one fixed prior belief
set.  The representation theorem uses it immediately
\cite{KatsunoMendelzon1991}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-agm-representation
present_destinations.title: AGM faithful-preorder representation for finite propositional belief sets
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For each consistent \(K\), a revision operation satisfies all eight postulates
in Table~\ref{tab:p08-agm-postulates} exactly when there is a total preorder
\(\preceq_K\) faithful to \(K\) such that, for every formula \(A\),
\[
 K*A=\operatorname{Th}\bigl(\min([A],\preceq_K)\bigr).
\]
If \(A\) is inconsistent, the minimum set is empty and its theory is the
inconsistent theory, as required by the consistency postulate.  The original
AGM partial-meet representation instead constructs contraction and obtains
revision through Levi; the two presentations agree under their stated
propositional representation hypotheses
\cite{AlchourronGardenforsMakinson1985}.  Database update, iterated revision,
and belief-base revision require different or additional postulates and are not
included.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-sdl
present_destinations.title: Standard deontic logic
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Standard deontic logic \(\mathsf{SDL}\) is normal modal logic \(\mathsf{KD}\)
with \(O A\) read as ``it ought to be that \(A\)'' and
\(\mathsf P_O A\defeq\neg O\neg A\). Relationally, \(O\) is box over a serial
ideal-alternative relation. The name is necessary to fix this monadic normal
system rather than deontic logic generally. It stands as a formal modal
calculus/semantics, differs through seriality and the D axiom
\(OA\to\mathsf P_OA\), and is used as the baseline for contrary-to-duty failures
\cite{VonWright1951,McNamara2006}.
\index{standard deontic logic}\index{obligation operator}\index{permission operator}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-dyadic-obligation
present_destinations.title: Best-world semantics for dyadic obligation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A dyadic deontic model adds, at each world \(w\), a total preorder
\(\preceq_w\) on
\(R(w)=\{u\in W:wRu\}\), oriented so that
\(u\preceq_w v\) means that \(u\) is at least as ideal as \(v\).  Its strict
part is
\[
 u\prec_w v
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 u\preceq_w v\ \text{and}\ v\not\preceq_w u.
\]
The preorder is \emph{smooth on definable candidate sets} when, for every
formula \(B\) and every \(u\in R(w)\cap[B]\), either no member of
\(R(w)\cap[B]\) is strictly more ideal than \(u\), or there is
\(v\in R(w)\cap[B]\) such that \(v\prec_w u\) and no
\(z\in R(w)\cap[B]\) satisfies \(z\prec_w v\).  Define, for every \(B\),
\[
 \operatorname{Best}_w(B)
 =\{u\in R(w)\cap[B]:
       \nexists v\in R(w)\cap[B]\ (v\prec_w u)\}.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{Best}_w(B)=\varnothing\) when there is no accessible
\(B\)-world, while smoothness makes it nonempty whenever the candidate set is
nonempty.  Put
\[
 M,w\models O(A\mid B)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{Best}_w(B)\ne\varnothing
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \operatorname{Best}_w(B)\subseteq[A].
\]
The existence conjunct makes an obligation with an impossible condition false
in this selected presentation; a vacuous alternative would be a different
dyadic semantics.
The name is necessary because \(B\) is a parameter of the ideality comparison,
not the antecedent of material implication.  It names a binary modality under
the displayed preference semantics, not dyadic deontic logic in general.  It
differs from \(O(B\to A)\) and is used to state
\(O(\neg B\mid\neg A)\) as a violation-triggered obligation without detaching
it in ideal \(A\)-worlds \cite{Hansson1969}.
\index{dyadic deontic logic}\index{conditional obligation}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-stalnaker-conditional
present_destinations.title: Selection-function counterfactual
present_destinations.declaration_text:
In a Stalnaker model, a selection function has type
\(f:W\times(\mathcal P(W)\setminus\{\varnothing\})\to W\) and satisfies
\(f(w,X)\in X\).  Put
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 M,f(w,[A])\models B.
\]
Thus impossible antecedents are vacuously true in this selected presentation;
for nonempty antecedents exactly one world is selected.  Centering is the
additional condition \(w\in X\Rightarrow f(w,X)=w\), not part of selection
alone.  The definition is needed because the
connective \(>\) is not material implication and because uniqueness is stronger
than merely having a set of closest worlds. It stands as a semantic clause,
differs from Lewis's sphere semantics through unique selection, and is used to
test conditional excluded middle \cite{Stalnaker1968}.
\index{counterfactual conditional}\index{selection-function semantics}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-lewis-conditional
present_destinations.title: Lewis sphere counterfactual
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A Lewis model assigns each world \(w\) a nonempty family
\(\mathcal S_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathcal S_w\) is linearly ordered by inclusion;
  \item for every \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\),
    \(\bigcup\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\); and
  \item if \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\) and
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\ne\varnothing\), then
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\).
\end{enumerate}
Write \(U_w=\bigcup\mathcal S_w\).  The variably strict clause is
\[
 M,w\models A\Box\!\!\to B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]\cap U_w=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\land S\cap[A]\subseteq[B]\bigr).
\]
This clause does not require a least \(A\)-permitting sphere.  The system is
\emph{weakly centered} when, for every \(w\),
\[
 w\in U_w
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \forall S\in\mathcal S_w\,
   (S\ne\varnothing\to w\in S),
\]
and \emph{centered} when
\(\{w\}\in\mathcal S_w\) for every \(w\).  Nesting makes centering imply weak
centering.  Lewis's \(\mathsf V\), \(\mathsf{VW}\), and \(\mathsf{VC}\)
use, respectively, arbitrary sphere systems of the displayed kind, weakly
centered systems, and centered systems.  The \emph{limit assumption} is the
further condition that, whenever \([A]\cap U_w\ne\varnothing\),
\[
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w\,
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\ \land\
   \forall T\in\mathcal S_w\,
     (T\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\to S\subseteq T)\bigr).
\]
None of these centering clauses entails the limit assumption.  The sphere
definition is needed because there may be several equally close worlds or no
minimal sphere. It stands as a comparative-similarity semantics, differs from
unique selection, and is used for limit-assumption and centering distinctions
\cite{Lewis1973}.
\index{sphere semantics}\index{limit assumption}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-ck-semantics
present_destinations.title: CK selection and premise semantics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A \emph{CK selection model} assigns each world \(w\) a function
\(F_w:\mathcal P(W)\to\mathcal P(W)\), with no requirement that
\(F_w(X)\subseteq X\), and sets
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_w([A])\subseteq[B].
\]
If \(F_w(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), every conditional with an impossible
antecedent is true at \(w\); basic CK does not impose that additional condition.
Equivalently, a \emph{premise-semantics presentation} assigns a relation
\(\mathcal N_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\times\mathcal P(W)\) and reads
\(A>B\) as \(([A],[B])\in\mathcal N_w\), where each fixed-antecedent section
is a principal filter: for some core \(K_w(X)\subseteq W\),
\((X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w\) exactly when \(K_w(X)\subseteq Y\).  Such a section
contains \(W\) and is closed under intersection and supersets.  The two
presentations correspond by
\[
 (X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_w(X)\subseteq Y.
\]
The names are necessary because assigning a consequent-test set to an
antecedent proposition and relating premise/conclusion propositions are
different semantic data.  They
name model presentations for the same basic logic, not object-language
connectives.  Their nonredundancy is visible in the displayed conversion, and
the CK completeness theorem uses it \cite{Chellas1975}.  The absent inclusion
condition is load-bearing: adding \(F_w(X)\subseteq X\) validates the identity
schema \(A>A\), which belongs to stronger conditional systems rather than
basic \(\mathsf{CK}\).
\index{conditional logic!CK}\index{premise semantics!conditional logic}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-ck-completeness
present_destinations.title: Soundness and completeness of conditional logic CK
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The theoremhood calculus on
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-conditional-ck]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-conditional-ck}}
is sound and complete for the CK selection models, equivalently the
fixed-antecedent premise semantics, of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-ck-semantics}.

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-vc-completeness
present_destinations.title: Soundness and completeness of Lewis VC, or C1
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Lewis's centered variably strict system \(\mathsf{VC}\), called
\(\mathsf{C1}\) in the cited alternative nomenclature, is presented on
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-counterfactual-vc]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-counterfactual-vc}}
and is sound and complete for the centered sphere semantics of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-lewis-conditional}.  The source's limit-free clause is
the one printed there; no least-sphere assumption is smuggled into the theorem
\cite{Wen2019}.

present_destinations.label: def:p10-boolean-algebra
present_destinations.title: Boolean algebra, filter, ideal, and ultrafilter
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive lattice
\((B,\wedge,\vee,\neg,0,1)\) satisfying
\(a\wedge\neg a=0\) and \(a\vee\neg a=1\).
The one-element algebra with \(0=1\) is allowed.
The order is \(a\leq b\) exactly when \(a\wedge b=a\).
A filter \(F\subseteq B\) contains \(1\), is upward closed, and is
closed under binary meets; it is proper when \(0\notin F\).
An ideal contains \(0\), is downward closed, and is closed under
binary joins; it is proper when it excludes \(1\).
An ultrafilter is a maximal proper filter. Equivalently, it is a
filter containing exactly one of \(a,\neg a\) for every \(a\), as
proved in Lemma~\ref{thm:p10-ultrafilter-separation}. These terms are
needed because algebraic truth assignments, deductively closed theories, and
prime points of a dual space occupy different levels. They stand as algebraic
structures and subsets and are used in Stone representation and the
Lindenbaum--Tarski construction.
\index{Boolean algebra}\index{filter!Boolean algebra}\index{ultrafilter}\index{ideal}

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-ultrafilter-separation
present_destinations.title: Ultrafilter dichotomy and separation
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A proper filter \(U\) is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every
\(a\in B\), exactly one of \(a,\neg a\) belongs to \(U\).
Consequently,
\[
 a\vee b\in U\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in U\text{ or }b\in U.
\]
Assuming BPIT, if \(F\) is a filter and \(b\notin F\), there is an
ultrafilter \(U\supseteq F\) with \(b\notin U\).
In particular, each nonzero element belongs to an ultrafilter,
and distinct Boolean elements are separated by an ultrafilter.
The trivial Boolean algebra has no ultrafilters.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-stone-representation
present_destinations.title: Stone representation theorem
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Assuming BPIT, \(X_B\) is a Stone space and
\[
 \beta_B:B\longrightarrow\operatorname{Clop}(X_B),
 \qquad \beta_B(a)=\widehat a,
\]
is a Boolean-algebra isomorphism.
In particular, it is an injective Boolean homomorphism onto all
clopen subsets, not merely onto a Boolean subalgebra of them.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-stone-duality
present_destinations.title: Functorial Stone duality
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Assuming BPIT, the inverse-image assignments are well-defined
contravariant functors
\[
 \mathsf{BA}\ \xrightarrow{\ X\ }\ \mathsf{Stone},
 \qquad
 \mathsf{Stone}\ \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Clop}\ }\ \mathsf{BA}.
\]
The Boolean isomorphisms \(\beta_B\) and homeomorphisms
\(\varepsilon_X\) are natural: for \(h:B\to C\) and \(g:X\to Y\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Clop}(X(h))\circ\beta_B&=\beta_C\circ h,\\
 X(\operatorname{Clop}(g))\circ\varepsilon_X&=\varepsilon_Y\circ g.
\end{aligned}
\]
They satisfy the identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
 X(\beta_B)\circ\varepsilon_{X_B}&=1_{X_B},\\
 \operatorname{Clop}(\varepsilon_X)\circ
                 \beta_{\operatorname{Clop}(X)}
      &=1_{\operatorname{Clop}(X)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the categories are contravariantly equivalent.
Every continuous map \(f:X_C\to X_B\) arises from a unique Boolean
homomorphism \(h:B\to C\) by \(f=X(h)\).

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-countable-atomless-uniqueness
present_destinations.title: Uniqueness of the countable atomless Boolean algebra
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Any two nontrivial countable atomless Boolean algebras are isomorphic.
More generally, every isomorphism between finite subalgebras of two
such algebras extends to an isomorphism of the whole algebras.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-cantor-cylinder-algebra
present_destinations.title: Existence through clopen cylinders
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Cantor space is nonempty, compact, and Hausdorff.
Every clopen subset of \(K\) is a finite union of cylinders of
one common length, so
\[
 \operatorname{Clop}(K)=\mathcal B_{\rm cyl}.
\]
This is a nontrivial countably infinite atomless Boolean algebra.
The finite subalgebras \(\mathcal B_n\) have
\(2^{2^n}\) elements; their inclusions split every cylinder atom
\([s]\) into \([s0]\) and \([s1]\).
Their union is also the direct limit of this inclusion sequence.
Consequently there exists exactly one nontrivial countable atomless
Boolean algebra up to isomorphism.

present_destinations.label: thm:p10-atoms-isolated
present_destinations.title: Atoms and isolated Stone points
present_destinations.declaration_text:
Assume the Boolean prime ideal theorem, as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:p10-stone-representation}.
For every Boolean algebra \(B\), its atoms correspond bijectively
to the isolated points of \(X_B\).
The atom \(p\) corresponds to the principal ultrafilter
\[
 U_p=\{b\in B:p\leq b\},\qquad \widehat p=\{U_p\}.
\]
In particular, \(B\) is atomless exactly when \(X_B\) has no
isolated points.  If \(B\) is finite and nontrivial with \(k\)
atoms, then \(X_B\) is a discrete \(k\)-point space and
\(|B|=2^k\).
